\chapter{The Field}
\label{ch:ka-field}
\hlchaptermodality{66}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a Kannada field and its crop, and take my leave of the village that grew it.}

Complete KA-C66-harvest and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hola]{\kn{ಹೊಲ} (hola) — a field}

\label{lesson:KA-C66-field}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{nambike} mean, and what did \emph{saujanya} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹೊಲ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೊಲ}} (\emph{hola}) — \textquotedblleft{}a field\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಹೊಲ} is inherited, and it is the dry field — ground that is ploughed and planted and waits on the \kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ} for its water.

It lies past the edge of the \kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ}, along the \kn{ದಾರಿ} you learned to ask for, and it is where the \kn{ರೈತ} is when he is not at home.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five field words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hola}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{hola}, then \emph{raita}, and say which one works the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಹೊಲ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a field\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hullu]{\kn{ಹುಲ್ಲು} (hullu) — grass}

\label{lesson:KA-C66-grass}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{hola} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹುಲ್ಲು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹುಲ್ಲು}} (\emph{hullu}) — \textquotedblleft{}grass\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಹುಲ್ಲು} is what comes up on ground nobody planted, and it is why the \kn{ಹಸು} and the \kn{ಮೇಕೆ} from the animal chapter are walked out of the yard at all.

Say it carefully against \kn{ಹಲ್ಲು}, the tooth-word. One vowel sign separates them and the rest of the two words is identical. It is the closest pair this book has handed you, and the good news is that the \kn{ಹಸು} eats the one with your teeth.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hullu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{hallu}, then \emph{hullu}, and say which one is in your mouth
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಹುಲ್ಲು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grass\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhatta]{\kn{ಭತ್ತ} (bhatta) — paddy, rice in the husk}

\label{lesson:KA-C66-paddy}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{hullu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಭತ್ತ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಭತ್ತ}} (\emph{bhatta}) — \textquotedblleft{}paddy, rice in the husk\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಭತ್ತ} completes a set you have been assembling since the water-and-rice chapter. One plant, three names, and Kannada keeps them strictly apart: \kn{ಭತ್ತ} standing in the \kn{ಹೊಲ}, \kn{ಅಕ್ಕಿ} once it is husked and in the sack, \kn{ಅನ್ನ} once it is cooked and on the plate.

English makes do with \emph{rice} for all three and adds a word when it must. Kannada gives each stage its own name, and a speaker who used the wrong one would be understood but marked as not from here.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhatta}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bhatta}, then \emph{akki}, then \emph{anna}, in that order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಭತ್ತ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}paddy, rice in the husk\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[beḷe]{\kn{ಬೆಳೆ} (beḷe) — a crop}

\label{lesson:KA-C66-crop}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bhatta} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬೆಳೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬೆಳೆ}} (\emph{beḷe}) — \textquotedblleft{}a crop\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಬೆಳೆ} is the general one: \kn{ಭತ್ತ} is a \kn{ಬೆಳೆ}, and so is everything else a \kn{ಹೊಲ} is put to. Native, and made from the everyday word for growing — so the same shape names the growing and the grown thing, the way \kn{ನೂಲು} named the thread and the spinning.

The chain runs the length of this book by now. A \kn{ಬೀಜ} goes into the ground, the \kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ} arrives, and a \kn{ಬೆಳೆ} stands in the \kn{ಹೊಲ}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{beḷe}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bīja}, then \emph{beḷe}, and say which one comes first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬೆಳೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a crop\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[suggi]{\kn{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ} (suggi) — the harvest}

\label{lesson:KA-C66-harvest}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{beḷe} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ}} (\emph{suggi}) — \textquotedblleft{}the harvest\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ} is not only the cutting. It is the season, and it is the mood of the season — the stretch of weeks when the \kn{ಬೆಳೆ} is in and there is enough, and Karnataka's harvest festival carries the word in its name.

So these five words end where a farming year does. It opened with \kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ} in the seasons chapter, ran through the \kn{ಬೀಜ} and the \kn{ಬೆಳೆ}, and arrives at the \kn{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ} with the \kn{ಹೊಲ} empty and the house full.

Which makes this the right place to take your leave of the \kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ}. You can name what it grows now, and thank the people who grew it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \kn{ಹೊಲ}, \kn{ಹುಲ್ಲು}, \kn{ಭತ್ತ}, \kn{ಬೆಳೆ}, \kn{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ}. A field, what grows on it, and the season that takes it in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{suggi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{hōgi baruttēne}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the harvest\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
